Building the Bag: eBay, ChatGPT and Google searches helped Ross Steelman make PGA Tour

Published

3 weeks ago

on

Oct 21, 2026

By

Alistair Cameron
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 13:40
Instaread

PGA Tour pros have an abundance of help finding the best bag setup to help them succeed. They have everything from Tour trucks stocked with the latest technology to highly trained reps who can diagnose what’s working and what’s not. But for Ross Steelman, his setup is a little different.

Steelman is one of the newest members of the PGA Tour, after securing his card this season on the Korn Ferry Tour as the No. 1 in the points list. At a glance, his setup doesn’t look out of the norm, but digging deeper reveals a story about how Steelman ended up playing what he does that’s unlike any other.

Starting with the driver, Steelman plays the TaylorMade Qi4D at 8 degrees. Pretty standard on Tour, but Steelman’s has a personal touch. The 25-year-old used a Sharpie to cover up the reflective strip that surrounds the face of the driver. It’s also fitted with a Mitsubishi Chemical Diamana PD 60 X. It’s a shaft that was released at the start of the decade, and in fact, Steelman purchased a used one off eBay due to the lack of availability, as it is an older model.

“I really enjoy, like, finding kind of niche clubs on my own, and just making them work,” Steelman said. “You know, we are very fortunate to get any golf club we want for free, but there’s just something romantic about finding it yourself and kind of having hands-on experience with how it is, and just a lot of trust that goes into it, knowing that I’m the one that did, you know, everything to make it work.”

Steelman admitted that his driver did have to be re-bonded earlier in the year as his build job wasn’t up to par. It did the job, though, with Steelman ranking first on Tour for Strokes Gained: Off the tee.

Moving on to the 3-wood, his Qi4D 15-degree has the same backstory, having found the Diamana PD 70 X on eBay as well, and built up the clubs himself.

“Length … who knows, I kept cutting and re-gripping until it felt right,” Steelman told GolfWRX about the builds.

Steelman’s iron setup is where things really get unique. Liking the way the Diamana PD shafts moved through his golf swing, Steelman used ChatGPT’s artificial intelligence to determine a similar-feeling iron shaft that he could test on his TaylorMade P7CBs.

“It told me to try Steelfiber, so I bought one and put it in an old 8 iron, and it was perfect,” Steelman told GolfWRX about his AI fitting. “Super light, right amount of give, very muted feel through the turf, which I love.”

Steelman experimented with a single 8-iron build with the Aerotech SteelFiber 110CW, and instantly saw the results. With a full set in play, Steelman says he was 160-under-par over an eight-event stretch. Building the irons himself, Steelman says that each club is a different swingweight. Starting each club at D0, Steelman adds lead tape to some of them “purely based on the feel of each head.”

Speaking of lead tape, Steelman uses it as a label on his wedges to note how many rounds of golf he’s played with each wedge. It helps him determine when he needs to trade them out for a new set.

“It’s about 16-20 before it’s time for a new one,” Steelman thinks.

Steelman continues his use of pre-owned golf gear with a putter which he bought off eBay too: a TaylorMade Rossa TP by Kia Ma.

“I was using an old red Spider which I really liked but wasn’t putting very well … searched ‘TaylorMade milled blade’ and bought the first one that came up,” Steelman said. “It was 34 inches, so I extended it, slapped a piece of lead tape on the bottom, and haven’t hit a putt with another putter since.”

Before adding the blade to his bag, Steelman ranked 112th on Tour in SG: Putting. He ended the season 29th, gaining on average 0.338 strokes on the greens each round. TaylorMade Tour reps Scott Boulware and James Holley are the only ones who know the exact specs of the putter and are under strict instructions not to tell Steelman.

“Sometimes things are best not known,” said Steelman, and if you’re looking to pick one up off eBay, you better move past because Steelman is buying plenty of backups.

Check out Steelman’s full WITB and specs below:

Driver: TaylorMade Qi4D 8 upright 1 click towards lower 2° sleeve
Shaft: Diamana PD 60x 45.6” no tipping. D1 swing weight
3-wood: TaylorMade Qi4D 15 upright 2 clicks towards lower 2° sleeve
Shaft: Diamana PD 70x 0.5” tipped. D0 swing weight
Hybrid: TaylorMade Qi10 Tour 19.5 upright setting 1.5° sleeve
Shaft: Modus GOST 95 x…D3 swing weight
Irons: TaylorMade 4-9 P7CB
Shafts: Steelfiber 110x CW D0-D2 swing weigh
Wedges: TaylorMade MG5 SB (46,50,56) & SX 60
Shafts: Steelfiber 110x C46, 50,50) & 125x C56, 60,60). 46 & 50 are D1, 56 & 60 are D4.
Putter: TaylorMade Rossa Daytona Milled TP

Time capsules, Frankenstein putters & lead tape: Inside the bags of PGA Tour Champions

Published

5 days ago

on

Nov 5, 2026

By

Alistair Cameron

While the regular PGA Tour is often dominated by equipment contracts and the newest retail releases, the PGA Tour Champions represents pure golf gear anarchy. Free from these somewhat restrictive marketing mandates, the 50-and-over circuit has quietly become a hotbed for weird, wonderful, and heavily customized golf equipment.

Out here, players game whatever delivers results – whether that means decade-old relics, surgical lab experiments, or thick slabs of lead tape. Here is a look inside some of the wildest setups currently competing on the senior tour.

Lead tape and tales of time: Tag Ridings

Tag Ridings’ bag looks less like a modern tour setup and more like Andrew Von Lossow’s free time. Spanning distinct eras of golf manufacturing and bonded by heavy lead tape customization, his gear includes:

  • Quarter-century-old flatstick: A classic Bobby Grace MacGregor putter dating back roughly 25 years.

  • Vintage wedges: Early-2010s Titleist Vokey SM4 wedges featuring heavily layered lead tape across the back.

  • The juxtaposition: At the top of the bag sits a modern and forgiving Callaway Quantum Max driver displaying arguably one of the most unusual weight-tuning jobs ever spotted on tour: multiple thick wraps of lead tape plastered directly around the hosel adapter itself, completely locking out any adjustability.

He will not change: Henrik Stenson

Then some players find a winning formula and refuse to change. Henrik Stenson’s bag remains anchored by long-standing staples:

  • Legacy irons: Callaway’s Japan- and Europe-released irons that Roger Cleveland had a say in the design. 

  • The famous fairway wood: His iconic Callaway Diablo Octane 3-wood, paired with the exact Grafalloy Blue X shaft he relied on to capture The Open Championship.

  • The supporting metal: A Callaway Rogue Sub Zero 5-wood fitted with an Oban Kiyoshi Tour shaft.

The relentless tinkerer: Padraig Harrington

On the opposite end of the spectrum is three-time major champion Pádraig Harrington, a golfer famous for tweaking his gear to fit his demands.

While his greatest triumphs came with an Odyssey Two-Ball blade putter, his current flatstick is a pure “Frankenstein” build:

  • At a glance: An original OG Two-Ball mallet chassis.

  • Frankenstein insert: A transplanted modern Odyssey Ai-Dual face insert.

  • Cavity fillings: Custom epoxy applied straight into the sole cavities to likely add weight and affect the way the putter sits at address.

Trend setter turns reverser: Michael Block

Customization and tour-inspired builds also travel both ways. Club professional sensation Michael Block, who’s now a regular on the senior tour, was spotted gaming a Ping Scottsdale TR Ally Blue onset putter: 

  • Major influence: Featuring a meticulous, grid-like lead tape pattern covering the entire sole, echoing setup modifications popularised by U.S. Open winner Wyndham Clark.

Wyndham Clark and more — Lead Tape Report’s top 5 from the 2026 season

Published

7 days ago

on

Nov 3, 2026

By

Andrew Von Lossow

With the season winding down, we at the Lead Tape Report felt the time was right to take a backward look at some of the slabs we saw (and loved!) in 2026.

Wyndham Clark’s Pro Shop Pick-Up

This one putter purchase was a favorite to me because it’s something you would see on a Saturday morning game. One of your friends has a new putter. “Where did you get that?” They say they just picked it up in the shop, and it is time for its maiden voyage. Amplify the stakes and tournament setting, and you have Wyndham Clark with this trial of his Bettinardi Antidote SB1. Clark made one of the most notable putter switches this season, and the results back it up with wins at the CJ Cup Byron Nelson, the U.S. Open, and the BMW Championship with his Ping Scottsdale TEC Ally Blue Onset putter. That all began with his win at the CJ Cup Byron Nelson.

Akshay’s Layers 

I really like the look of this Callaway Opus 60-degree wedge from Akshay. The reason is the layers of tape. While getting the feel of the club, you may need to increase the weight of the clubhead. Here you can see he and his team went back to the drawing board a few times before making the decision. Cap that off with a raw finish on the wedge; it is ready for tournament action. Hitting so many different types of shots with a lob wedge, this club needs to check the boxes from the fairway, rough, bunkers, and short-sided shots.

Former Champion Returns With Long-Time Accomplice

Graeme McDowell qualified for the US Open this last year at Shinnecock. I cannot help but notice the long-time putter style he has used with his Odyssey White Hot #7, the original #7 at that, with a plumber’s neck and half-moon mallet shape. The lead tape has been on the putter so long there is no issue seeing the logo on the sole. 

Hideki’s Driver

There are many things for me to highlight when it comes to Hideki. This one is the leader in the clubhouse right now for a recap with two things in focus. The custom driver face on this Srixon ZXi RKT LS makes it appear smaller at address, and the small piece of lead tape at the end of the grip. The level of feel and detail that Matsuyama has is something that is to the nth degree and extremely honed in for his equipment and his specifications.

The Glory of Tag Ridings

Tag Riding stole the lead tape show at the Simmons Bank Championship on the PGA Tour Champions last week. He has customized his clubs for years, and it was a bit, but our Tour Photographer Greg Moore tracked them down. The lead tape on the hosel of the club, more pieces throughout the woods, irons, wedges, and putter covered. This shows complete ownership of how the club should feel in his hands and makes for a set that fits his feel.

Ping G450 drivers hit conforming list along with new mini driver contender

Published

1 week ago

on

Nov 2, 2026

By

Alistair Cameron

The USGA and R&A conforming club list just received a notable update. Alongside the arrival of the flagship Ping G450 lineup – which was widely anticipated – Ping is officially entering the mini driver category with the inclusion of a G450 MiniMax head.

Mini drivers have surged into the mainstream over the past few seasons, and while Ping has had a prototype option on Tour, the retail option for a fairway-finder has been the “thriver.” In short, (no pun intended) a higher-lofted head on a shorter shaft.

The Lineup: Max, LST, SFT and a new contender

The submissions confirm that Ping is sticking to its proven family structure for full-size heads while potentially introducing a compact alternative off the tee:

  • G450 Max: A high-MOI model built for maximum forgiveness and stability. (Lofts: 9°, 10.5°, 12°).

  • G450 LST: The lower-spinning profile engineered for faster swing speeds. (Lofts: 7.5°, 9°, 10.5°).

  • G450 SFT: The dedicated slice-correction option with internal draw bias for a straighter flight. (Lofts: 9°, 10.5°).

  • G450 MiniMax: A 13-degree option, with potentially a smaller head size.

What the black-and-white images could reveal

While Ping has yet to release internal specs, sole markings and geometry point toward several notable design cues:

  • First look at Fastflex: There’s a new buzzword in town, and it is named Fastflex. Located behind the face, the design looks similar to that of the TaylorMade Speed Pocket, which reduces spin and protects ball speeds on low-face strikes for consistent performance, even on off-center hits.

  • Carbonfly wrap and rear weighting: Visible rear weight ports indicate movable perimeter weighting across the MAX and LST lines, with the SFT altering the amount of draw bias.

  • The MiniMax inclusion: Rather than a niche tour-only prototype, the “MiniMax” moniker signals that Ping is designing its mini driver around a higher MOI profile. This could be bigger than the standard 280-300cc head size.

Clubs appearing on the USGA conforming list mark the start of the tour validation window, meaning Ping staffers (and others) will likely begin testing and bagging the G450 family during upcoming late-season stops and early tour swings.
